t: Wireshark: What Wireshark Is: The Network's Microscope
title: Wireshark: What Wireshark Is: The Network's Microscope
description: Wireshark captures packets from an interface (via libpcap/Npcap) or reads capture files, then dissects them — Ethernet to IP to TCP to TLS to HTTP — presenting every field of every layer. The display filters (ip.addr == x, tcp.port == 443) slice millions of packets to the interesting few; Follow Stream reassembles conversations. It is the tool behind 'what is actually on the wire' — the ground truth of networks, used by every network engineer and incident responder.

title: Wireshark: Dissectors: Reading Every Layer
description: A dissector parses one protocol's bytes into named fields: the TCP dissector shows sequence numbers, flags, window sizes; the TLS dissector shows handshake messages and cipher suites. Wireshark chains them by port and heuristics. Writing a Lua dissector for a proprietary protocol is the power move — your weird industrial protocol becomes as readable as HTTP. Understanding dissectors is understanding that 'the network' is just agreed-upon byte layouts.
key_facts: Custom Lua dissectors for proprietary protocols

t: Wireshark: Display Filters: Finding the Needle
title: Wireshark: Display Filters: Finding the Needle
description: Capture everything, display the interesting: display filters (different from capture filters) query the dissected fields — 'tls.handshake.type == 1 and ip.addr == 10.0.0.5' shows one host's ClientHellos. Filter fluency is Wireshark fluency: the expert finds the three packets that matter in a million-packet capture in seconds. The filter expression is also documentation — save it with the analysis.

console.log('lens: tls.handshake.type==1 && ip.addr==10.0.0.5');
console.log('1,000,000 packets -> 14 ClientHellos (lens saved to case)');

title: Wireshark: Follow Stream: Reassembling Conversations
description: Follow TCP Stream reassembles the byte flow — the HTTP request and response as text, the full conversation. For incident response this is reading the mail: what did the client ask, what did the server return? Combined with decryption (with the session keys, where authorized), even TLS sessions become readable. The stream view turns packets into narrative.

t: Wireshark: Your First Capture: The Local Handshake
title: Wireshark: Your First Capture: The Local Handshake
description: The hello-world: capture on loopback, load a web page, stop, filter 'http', Follow Stream the request. You see the DNS query, the TCP handshake, the TLS ClientHello, the HTTP exchange — the internet's choreography, exposed. Every network engineer remembers this moment: the abstraction became bytes, and the bytes made sense.

t: Wireshark: Tactical PCAP: Capturing in the Field
title: Wireshark: Tactical PCAP: Capturing in the Field
description: Tactical capture means small, rugged, and disciplined: a field laptop or appliance capturing to ring buffers (never filling the disk), with capture filters limiting to the interesting traffic, time-synchronized for correlation. The captures come home for analysis. The discipline is capture hygiene — know what you captured, when, and under what authority — because field captures become evidence.

t: Wireshark: Wireless and IoT Capture: Beyond Ethernet
title: Wireshark: Wireless and IoT Capture: Beyond Ethernet
description: Wireshark captures more than Ethernet: Wi-Fi (with radiotap headers showing signal strength and channels), Bluetooth, Zigbee/802.15.4, and LoRa — the IoT and tactical protocols. Wireless capture needs monitor mode and the right adapters; the analysis needs the protocol dissectors. For field networks of sensors and radios, this is where the packets actually are.

t: Wireshark: Statistics: The Network's Vital Signs
title: Wireshark: Statistics: The Network's Vital Signs
description: Wireshark's statistics — protocol hierarchy, conversations, IO graphs — show the network's shape: what percentage is TLS, who talks to whom, when the spike happened. For incident response, the IO graph's spike is often the first indicator; the conversations list names the talkers. Statistics turn a capture from a pile of packets into a situation report.

t: Wireshark: Defensive Uses: The Network Witness
title: Wireshark: Defensive Uses: The Network Witness
description: Wireshark's defensive value is ground truth: during incidents, the capture shows what actually traversed the wire — the exfiltration, the C2 beaconing, the lateral movement. Network forensics reconstructs the attack from packets when logs are incomplete or untrustworthy. The capture is the witness that cannot be gaslit — bytes are bytes.

t: Wireshark: Encrypted Traffic Analysis Without Decryption
title: Wireshark: Encrypted Traffic Analysis Without Decryption
description: Even encrypted traffic leaks metadata: handshake fingerprints (JA3), SNI, certificate details, timing and size patterns. Wireshark plus the right dissectors reveals the shape of encrypted conversations — which is often enough for defensive triage (that host is beaconing to a new TLS endpoint every 60 seconds). The discipline is knowing what metadata can and cannot prove.

title: Wireshark: Debugging: The Protocol Misbehaves
description: Wireshark debugs protocols: the retransmission storm (congested or lossy path), the TLS handshake failure (cipher mismatch, expired cert — the alert message says which), the DNS that never answers. The expert reads the handshake like a conversation and spots where it went wrong. 'The network is slow' becomes 'the server's window never opens' — a diagnosis, not a complaint.

t: Wireshark: Capture Filters: BPF at the Source
title: Wireshark: Capture Filters: BPF at the Source
description: Capture filters (BPF syntax: 'tcp port 443') drop uninteresting packets during capture — essential for high-rate links where storing everything is impossible. The art is filtering enough to fit the disk but little enough to keep the evidence: when in doubt, capture more. BPF is also the language of the kernel's packet filter — the same technology class as eBPF, fittingly.

title: Wireshark: Testing: Validating Network Changes
description: Wireshark validates network work: before/after captures proving the migration worked, the firewall rule actually blocks, the QoS policy actually prioritizes. 'Trust but verify' with packets: the capture is the test result. Change windows get their captures; the captures get reviewed. Networks are too important for 'it should be fine'.

t: Wireshark: Real-World Pattern: Incident Packet Forensics
title: Wireshark: Real-World Pattern: Incident Packet Forensics
description: A complete pattern: the SOC detects beaconing, pulls the sealed field capture, filters to the suspect host, follows the streams, extracts the C2 protocol with a Lua dissector, and documents the indicators. The firewall blocks the C2; the re-capture proves silence. The case file holds captures, lenses, and the handling log — the incident as an evidenced narrative.

title: Wireshark: Mastery: The Packet Analyst's Playbook
